zonker:
How to tie a Zonker. Dan Byford's streamer pairs a flashy Mylar body with a strip of rabbit fur that pulses with every strip. Big trout and bass treat it like a wounded baitfish.

You'll need a four-X-long streamer hook, size two to eight. Black or white three-oh thread. Pearl or silver Mylar tubing for the body, a rabbit zonker strip for the wing, and a hen or grizzly hackle for the collar.

Step one. Build a short, tapered underbody with thread. Slide a piece of Mylar tubing over it and tie it down at both ends.

Step two. Lay the rabbit strip on top, skin side down. Tie it in at the bend, then again just behind the eye, so it runs along the back.

Step three. Wind a few turns of hackle as a collar, whip finish and coat the head.

Strip it with pauses, so the rabbit breathes in the water. It's a great fly for big trout and bass.

sculpzilla:
How to tie a Sculpzilla. Kelly Galloup's streamer uses a heavy tungsten cone and a trailing hook to get a sculpin imitation down to the bottom, where big brown trout hunt.

You'll need a shank or streamer hook with a trailing hook. A tungsten cone. Olive six-oh thread. A rabbit strip for the tail, and marabou or schlappen for the body.

Step one. Attach the trailing hook with a loop of wire or braid, then tie in the rabbit strip as the tail.

Step two. Palmer marabou or schlappen forward over the shank, stroking the fibers back with each turn.

Step three. Tie off right behind the cone and whip finish.

Strip it close to the bottom in rivers, with short, erratic pulls like a fleeing sculpin.

slumpbuster:
How to tie a Slumpbuster. John Barr designed this simple streamer to break a fishing slump, and it does. A sparkle body under a pine squirrel strip makes a slim baitfish that moves beautifully.

You'll need a four-X-long streamer hook, size four to ten. A tungsten cone and some lead-free wire. Olive six-oh thread. Sparkle braid or tinsel for the body, copper wire for the rib, and a pine squirrel zonker strip.

Step one. Slide on the cone, add a few wraps of lead-free wire, and push them up into the cone.

Step two. Start the thread, tie in the copper wire, and wrap a sparkle braid body up the shank.

Step three. Lay the squirrel strip on top, skin side down, and tie it in at the bend. Then bind it along the back with the copper rib, Matuka style.

Step four. Wind the rest of the strip two or three turns right behind the cone, as a collar.

Step five. Tie off and whip finish behind the cone.

Strip it along the banks and through runs. Olive, black and natural are the go-to colors.

mickey-finn:
How to tie a Mickey Finn. This bright yellow and red bucktail has been catching fish since the nineteen-thirties. It doesn't imitate anything in particular, but it's hard for a fish to ignore.

You'll need a four-X-long streamer hook, size four to twelve. Black six-oh thread. Flat silver tinsel for the body, oval silver tinsel for the rib, yellow and red bucktail for the wing, and a few strands of gold flash if you like.

Step one. Wrap a smooth flat silver tinsel body, and rib it with oval tinsel.

Step two. Tie in a small bunch of yellow bucktail on top, reaching just past the bend.

Step three. Add a bunch of red bucktail on top of that, then a larger bunch of yellow on top.

Step four. Build a neat black head, whip finish and varnish it.

Strip it fast for stocked trout, bass and pickerel, especially in colored water.

black-nosed-dace:
How to tie a Black Nosed Dace. Art Flick created this simple bucktail to imitate the little dace minnows in Catskill streams. The dark stripe down its side is the key feature.

You'll need a four-X-long streamer hook, size four to twelve. Black six-oh thread. A short piece of red yarn for the tail, silver tinsel for the body, and white, black and brown bucktail for the wing.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short red yarn tail, then wrap a smooth silver tinsel body.

Step two. Stack the wing in layers: white bucktail first, then a thin bunch of black, then brown on top.

Step three. Build a neat head and whip finish.

Strip it along the bottom, where real dace live.

gray-ghost:
How to tie a Gray Ghost. Carrie Stevens created this elegant streamer in Maine in the nineteen-thirties to imitate smelt. It's a challenging tie, but it's one of the most beautiful flies ever designed.

You'll need an eight-X-long streamer hook, size two to eight. Black six-oh thread. Orange floss and flat silver tinsel for the body. White bucktail and peacock herl for the belly. Golden pheasant crest and four gray saddle hackles for the wing, silver pheasant for the shoulders, and jungle cock for the cheeks.

Step one. Wrap a smooth orange floss body, and rib it with flat silver tinsel.

Step two. Turn the hook over, or reach underneath, and tie in a few strands of peacock herl and a sparse bunch of white bucktail as the belly.

Step three. On top, tie in a golden pheasant crest, then four gray saddle hackles as the wing.

Step four. Add a silver pheasant feather on each side as shoulders, and jungle cock as cheeks. Build a neat head, whip finish and varnish.

Troll it or strip it for landlocked salmon and brook trout, especially early in the season when smelt are running.

sparkle-minnow:
How to tie a Sparkle Minnow. Jeff Coffey's flashy little baitfish is just a marabou tail and a braided sparkle body behind a cone. It takes two minutes to tie, and smallmouth and trout love it.

You'll need a streamer hook, size four to eight. A tungsten cone. White or olive six-oh thread. Marabou with a few strands of flash for the tail, and sparkle minnow braid for the body.

Step one. Slide on the cone and start the thread. At the bend, tie in a marabou tail with a few strands of flash.

Step two. Tie in the sparkle braid and wrap it forward in touching turns to make a shiny body.

Step three. Tie it off and whip finish right behind the cone.

Strip it or swing it through rivers for smallmouth bass and trout.

meat-whistle:
How to tie a Meat Whistle. John Barr's jig-style streamer rides hook-point up and hops along the bottom like a crayfish or sculpin. Bass, and big trout, can't resist it.

You'll need a sixty-degree jig hook, size one-aught to four. A tungsten cone. Olive or black six-oh thread. Ice Dub or wire for a short body, a rabbit zonker strip, marabou for the collar, and rubber legs and flash.

Step one. Slide on the cone and start the thread, then wrap a short body of Ice Dub or wire.

Step two. Tie a rabbit strip on top, so it trails behind as the tail.

Step three. Add a few strands of flash and rubber legs on each side, then wind a marabou collar.

Step four. Tie off and whip finish behind the cone.

Hop it along the bottom for bass and trout, with pauses so it settles nose-down.

bunny-leech:
How to tie a Bunny Leech. It's made from nothing but rabbit strips, so it's simple, cheap and full of life. Every strip makes the fur pulse like a swimming leech.

You'll need a streamer hook, size two to ten. An optional cone or bead. Black six-oh thread, and two rabbit strips: one for the tail and one for the body.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a rabbit strip as the tail, about as long as the hook shank.

Step two. Tie in a second strip and wind it forward around the shank, stroking the fur back with each turn so it doesn't get trapped.

Step three. Tie it off behind the eye and whip finish.

Strip or twitch it near the bottom. Black, olive and purple are the classic colors.

matuka:
How to tie a Matuka. This New Zealand streamer binds its feather wing along the back with a wire rib, so the wing can't foul around the hook. It swims like a sculpin or a little bully fish.

You'll need a four-X-long streamer hook, size four to ten. Olive six-oh thread. Dubbing or chenille for the body, oval tinsel or wire for the rib, four matched hen or saddle hackles for the wing, and a matching hackle for the collar.

Step one. At the bend, tie in the rib, then wind a dubbed or chenille body up the shank.

Step two. Strip the fibers from the underside of the hackles, and lay them on top of the body as the wing.

Step three. Bind the wing down with the rib, working the wire forward between the fibers so they stand up like a fin.

Step four. Wind a hackle collar at the front and whip finish.

Fish it slowly near the bottom. It suggests sculpins, bullies and other small fish.
